analysis.one_liner: Requires business interruption insurers to cover losses from pandemics and government-ordered closures.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2020, never received a markup or floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 shutdowns, most business interruption policies excluded losses from viruses and government-ordered closures, so many shuttered businesses got no payout on policies they had been paying for. This bill would require insurers that sell business interruption coverage to also cover losses from a viral pandemic, a government-ordered closure or evacuation, or a public-safety power shut-off, on the same terms as other covered losses. It would also void existing policy exclusions for those events — unless the business owner agrees in writing to keep the exclusion, or accepts it after the insurer sends 30 days' notice of a premium increase.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses holding business interruption policies, which would be able to collect for pandemic shutdown losses instead of having claims denied under virus exclusions. Their employees and landlords benefit indirectly when kept-open or compensated businesses keep paying wages and rent.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every insurer offering business interruption coverage to make available coverage for losses from any viral pandemic, any government-ordered closure or evacuation, and any public-safety power shut-off, on terms not materially different from other covered losses [S2] [S3].

Voids existing policy exclusions for those events on the date of enactment, and voids any state approval of such exclusions, so businesses with policies in force could claim pandemic losses [S2] [S3].
Lets an insurer put the exclusion back only if the business owner signs a written authorization, or after 30 days' notice of a premium increase and the owner fails to pay it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Property and casualty insurers, which would have to pay claims on policies priced and written with pandemic exclusions. The cost would ultimately be spread to business customers through higher premiums, and insurers warned mandates like this could make coverage unaffordable or unavailable.

drawbacks.text: The bill works retroactively: it voids exclusions in contracts already signed and priced, obliging insurers to pay for a risk they never charged for. Insurers and some state regulators argued this could destabilize the industry and that a federal mandate would raise premiums for every policyholder [S3].

The mandate is to 'make available' coverage at a corresponding premium, not to provide it free — so in a shutdown, a business still had to pay more to actually be covered, and the bill's own text anticipates insurers raising premiums to reinstate exclusions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit was real and timely: businesses that had faithfully paid for interruption coverage were being denied claims over virus exclusions, and the bill would have honored those policies. The strongest honest objection is the design — rewriting signed contracts after the fact, without a federal backstop for insurers, could have pushed up premiums or led some insurers to stop offering the coverage at all. A better-designed version would have paired the mandate with a reinsurance or federal backstop, an idea that circulated in 2020 but was not in this bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on April 14, 2020, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 14, 2020, roughly a month after most states ordered businesses to close, by Rep. Mike Thompson with nine original cosponsors including one Republican, Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama [S3] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded [S5].
It ended with 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats, 1 Republican) and expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Property and casualty insurers came out ahead: by the time the bill died, the pandemic exclusions in existing policies remained enforceable, so claims for shutdown losses were largely denied. Small businesses that had paid premiums for interruption coverage were left to sue over their policies instead of collecting.

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in April 2020.

for.name: 1 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama, an original cosponsor).

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 14, 2020 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or floor consideration; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Property and casualty insurance industry
against.role: Insurers that sell business interruption coverage
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal mandates to pay pandemic business interruption claims, arguing virus exclusions were valid and that retroactive coverage would require premium increases and threaten solvency; pressed instead for a federal backstop or none at all.

sides.party_line_note: Support was mostly Democratic — 12 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored versus 1 of 197 House Republicans — and the Democratic-held committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Property and casualty insurers (business interruption line)
industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to pay pandemic and closure claims on existing policies and to offer such coverage going forward, a potential liability of tens of billions of dollars. Because insurers collected premiums for interruption coverage while writing exclusions that let them deny the very losses businesses suffered in 2020, their interest in keeping the exclusions ran against the businesses and workers the bill aimed to help.
Covered businesses would have been paid for shutdown losses instead of litigating denied claims, keeping wages and rent flowing. The bill never passed, so this benefit never arrived.
